'''Robert Morris Sapolsky''' (born April 6, 1957) is an American academic, neuroscientist, and [[primatologist]]. He is the John A. and Cynthia Fry Gunn Professor at [[Stanford University]], where he is also a professor of [[biology]], [[neurology]], and [[neurosurgery]]. Sapolsky's research has focused on [[neuroendocrinology]], particularly relating to stress. He is also a research associate with the [[National Museums of Kenya]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.edge.org/3rd_culture/bios/sapolsky.html |title=Robert Sapolsky |access-date=22 Feb 2009 |archive-date=September 7, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140907011254/http://edge.org/3rd_culture/bios/sapolsky.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Sapolsky was born in [[Brooklyn]], [[New York (state)|New York]], to Jewish immigrants from the [[Soviet Union]]. His father, Thomas Sapolsky, was an architect who renovated the restaurants [[Lüchow's]] and [[Lundy's Restaurant|Lundy's]].<ref name="foot">{{Cite news|first=Patricia Leigh|last=Brown|date=19 April 2001|title=At home with: Dr. Robert M. Sapolsky; Family Man With a Foot In the Veld|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|url-access=subscription|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/04/19/garden/at-home-with-dr-robert-m-sapolsky-family-man-with-a-foot-in-the-veld.html|access-date=25 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231017124126/https://www.nytimes.com/2001/04/19/garden/at-home-with-dr-robert-m-sapolsky-family-man-with-a-foot-in-the-veld.html|archive-date=17 October 2023|url-status=live}}</ref> Robert was raised as an [[Orthodox Judaism|Orthodox Jew]] and spent his time reading about and imagining living with silverback [[gorilla]]s. By age 12, Sapolsky was writing fan letters to [[primatologists]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sapolsky |first=Robert |title=A Primate's Memoir |publisher=Simon & Schuster |year=2001 |isbn=978-1-4165-9036-1 |location=New York, NY |pages=24–25 |language=English}}</ref> He attended [[John Dewey High School]] and by that time was reading textbooks on the subject and teaching himself [[Swahili language|Swahili]].<ref name=StanfordMag>{{cite web|last=Vaughan|first=Christopher|title=Going Wild A biologist gets in touch with his inner primate.|date=November 2001 |url=https://stanfordmag.org/contents/going-wild|work=Stanford Magazine|access-date=15 March 2019}}</ref>

Sapolsky is an [[atheist]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://news.stanford.edu/news/2007/march7/sapolskysr-030707.html | title=Robert Sapolsky discusses physiological effects of stress | publisher=Stanford University | work=News | date=March 7, 2007 | access-date=October 13, 2012 | author=Shwartz, Mark}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Robert Sapolsky's lecture about Biological Underpinnings of Religiosity | date=December 30, 2011 |via = [[YouTube]]|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4WwAQqWUkpI&t=4827 }}</ref> In his acceptance speech for the [[Emperor Has No Clothes Award]], Sapolsky said, "I was raised in an Orthodox household and I was raised devoutly religious up until around age thirteen or so. In my adolescent years one of the defining actions in my life was breaking away from all religious belief whatsoever."<ref name="BaB">{{cite web|url=https://ffrf.org/outreach/awards/item/19619-belief-and-biology |title=Belief and Biology|last=Sapolsky|first=Robert|date=April 2003|website=Freedom from Religion Foundation |access-date=July 27, 2023}}</ref>

In 1978, Sapolsky received his B.A., ''[[summa cum laude]]'', in [[biological anthropology]] from [[Harvard University]].<ref name="NIHBio">{{cite web |title=Sapolsky Lectures on Stress and Health, Oct. 28 in Masur Auditorium - The NIH Record -October 16, 2009 |url=https://nihrecord.nih.gov/newsletters/2009/10_16_2009/story7.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150511162913/http://nihrecord.nih.gov/newsletters/2009/10_16_2009/story7.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 11, 2015 |website=nihrecord.nih.gov}}</ref><ref name="TGCBio">{{cite web |title=Professor Robert Sapolsky Bio Page |url=https://www.thegreatcourses.com/professors/robert-sapolsky |website=www.thegreatcourses.com}}</ref> He then went to [[Kenya]] to study the social behaviors of [[baboons]] in the wild. When the [[Uganda–Tanzania War]] broke out in the neighboring countries, Sapolsky decided to travel into Uganda to witness the war up close, later commenting, "I was twenty-one and wanted adventure. [...] I was behaving like a late-adolescent male primate."{{sfn|Sapolsky|2007|p=87}} He went to Uganda's capital [[Kampala]], and from there to the border with [[Zaire]] (now the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]]), and then back to Kampala, witnessing some fighting,{{sfn|Sapolsky|2007|pp=87–88}} including the [[Fall of Kampala|Ugandan capital's conquest]] by the [[Tanzania]]n [[Tanzania People's Defence Force|army]] and its Ugandan rebel allies on April 10–11, 1979.{{sfn|Sapolsky|2007|p=88}} Sapolsky then returned to New York and studied at [[Rockefeller University]], where he received his [[Ph.D.]] in [[neuroendocrinology]]<ref name="NIHBio"/><ref name="TGCBio"/> working in the lab of [[endocrinology|endocrinologist]] [[Bruce McEwen]].

After the initial year-and-a-half [[field study]] in Africa, Sapolsky returned every summer for another 25 years to observe the same group of baboons, from the late 1970s to the early 1990s. He spent eight to ten hours a day for approximately four months each year recording the behaviors of these baboons.<ref name=StanfordConversation>{{cite web|title=Transcript of How I Write Conversation with Robert Sapolsky|url=http://www.stanford.edu/group/howiwrite/Transcripts/Sapolsky_transcript.html|publisher=Stanford University|access-date=20 August 2011}}</ref>

== Career ==
Sapolsky is the John A. and Cynthia Fry Gunn Professor at [[Stanford University]], holding joint appointments in several departments, including Biological Sciences, Neurology & Neurological Sciences, and Neurosurgery.<ref>{{Cite web|url= http://med.stanford.edu/profiles/Robert_Sapolsky|title=Stanford Univ. detail of Prof. Sapolsky|access-date=2007-07-27}}</ref>

As a [[neuroendocrinologist]], Sapolsky has focused his research on issues of [[Stress (biology)|stress]] and [[neuronal degeneration]], as well as on the possibilities of [[gene therapy|gene-therapy]] strategies for protecting susceptible [[neuron]]s from disease.<ref>{{Cite book|title= Stress, the Aging Brain, and the Mechanisms of Neuron Death (Bradford Books) |isbn = 0262193205|last1 = Sapolsky|first1 = Robert M.|year = 1992| publisher=MIT Press }}</ref> He is working on [[gene transfer|gene-transfer]] techniques to strengthen [[neuron]]s against the disabling effects of [[glucocorticoid]]s.<ref>{{cite web |title=Robert Sapolsky |url=https://carta.anthropogeny.org/users/robert-sapolsky |website=Center for Academic Research and Training in Anthropogeny (CARTA) |publisher=UC San Diego |access-date=29 December 2022}}</ref> Sapolsky spends time in Kenya every year studying a population of wild [[baboon]]s in order to identify the sources of stress in their environment, and the relationship between personality and patterns of stress-related disease in these animals.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.rockefeller.edu/news/1728-rockefeller-university-names-robert-sopolsky-2008-lewis-thomas-prize-winner|title=Rockefeller University names Robert Sapolsky 2008 Lewis Thomas Prize winner|date=May 19, 2009 |website= Rockefeller University News|language=en|access-date=2020-03-31}}</ref> More specifically, he studies the differences in [[cortisol]] levels between the [[Alpha (biology)|alpha]] male and female and the subordinates to determine stress level. An early but still relevant example of Sapolsky's studies of olive baboons is found in his 1990 ''[[Scientific American]]'' article "Stress in the Wild".<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Sapolsky | first1 = Robert M | year = 1990 | title = Stress in the Wild | journal = Scientific American | volume = 262 | issue = 1 | pages = 106–13 | jstor = 24996650 | doi = 10.1038/scientificamerican0190-116 | pmid = 2294581 | bibcode = 1990SciAm.262a.116S }}</ref> He has also written about neurological impairment and the [[insanity defense]] within the [[American legal system]].<ref>"[https://www.nytimes.com/2007/03/11/magazine/11Neurolaw.t.html?pagewanted=all The Brain on the Stand]," ''New York Times Magazine''</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite journal | pmid = 15590619 | doi=10.1098/rstb.2004.1547 | volume=359 | issue=1451 | title=The frontal cortex and the criminal justice system | pmc=1693445 | journal=Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci | pages=1787–96 | last1 = Sapolsky | first1 = RM| year=2004 }}</ref>

Sapolsky is also interested in the role of [[Schizotypal personality disorder|schizotypal disorders]] in the emergence and development of [[shamanism]] and of the major [[Western religions]]. In this context, he has noted similarities between [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|obsessive-compulsive]] behavior and religious [[ritual]]s.<ref name="BaB" /><ref>{{Cite book |last= Sapolsky |first=Robert M. |chapter=Circling the Blanket for God |title=The Trouble with Testosterone: and Other Essays on the Biology of the Human Predicament |publisher= A Touchstone Book, Simon & Schuster 2017 |access-date=September 5, 2023}}</ref>

Sapolsky has vigorously argued for a [[Determinism|deterministic]] view of human behavior. According to him, "there is no [[free will]], or at least that there is much ''less'' free will than generally assumed when it really matters".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Sapolsky |first=Robert |title=Determined: A Science of Life without Free Will |publisher=Penguin Press |location=New York |year=2023 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Sv2nEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA13&lpg=PA13 13] | isbn=9780525560975 |language=English}}</ref> Sapolsky argues that human actions are determined by neurobiology, hormones, childhood, and [[personal life|life]]-circumstances.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Reese |first=Hope |date= October 18, 2023 |title=A Conversation With: Robert Sapolsky Doesn't Believe in Free Will. (But Feel Free to Disagree.) |work= The New York Times |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2023/10/16/science/free-will-sapolsky.html |access-date=22 Oct 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Sapolsky |first=Robert M. |chapter=Biology, the Criminal Justice System, and (Oh, Why Not?) Free Will |title=Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst |publisher=Penguin Press |location=New York |year= 2017 |pages=552–583 |isbn=978-1-594-20507-1 |url-access=registration |url= https://archive.org/details/BehaveTheBiologyOfHumansAtOurBestAndWorst_201812 }}</ref>

Sapolsky has received numerous honors and awards for his work, including a [[MacArthur Fellows Program|MacArthur Fellowship]] in 1987,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.macfound.org/site/c.lkLXJ8MQKrH/b.1142695/k.2A0E/Fellows_List__July_1987.htm|title=MacArthur Fellows List - July 1987|access-date=2008-03-24|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080419034630/http://www.macfound.org/site/c.lkLXJ8MQKrH/b.1142695/k.2A0E/Fellows_List__July_1987.htm|archive-date=2008-04-19}}</ref> an [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation|Alfred P. Sloan]] Fellowship, and the Klingenstein Fellowship in Neuroscience.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://mc.vanderbilt.edu/reporter/index.html?ID=5416 |title=Talk to probe roots of stress (03/16/07) |website=mc.vanderbilt.edu |access-date=2020-03-31 }}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Sapolsky was also awarded the [[National Science Foundation]] [[Presidential Young Investigator Award]],<ref name=":0" /> the Young Investigator of the Year Awards from the [[Society for Neuroscience]], the International Society for Psychoneuroendocrinology, and the [[Biological Psychiatry|Biological Psychiatry Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.middlebury.edu/newsroom/archive/2008/node/111715 |title=Science writer Robert Sapolsky to speak about coping with stress April 10|date=2009-12-17|website=Middlebury|language=en|access-date=2020-03-31}}</ref>

In 2007, Sapolsky received the [[John P. McGovern (physician)|John P. McGovern]] Award for Behavioral Science, awarded by the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name="AAAS">{{cite web |url=http://archives.aaas.org/awards.php?a_id=16 |access-date=22 Feb 2009 |title=About AAAS: John McGovern Lecture |archive-date=September 27, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927012448/http://archives.aaas.org/awards.php?a_id=16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The following year, he received [[Wonderfest]]'s [[Carl Sagan Prize for Science Popularization]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://wonderfest.org/sagan-prize/sagan-prize-recipients/ |title=Sagan Prize Recipients |work=wonderfest.org |year=2011 |access-date=September 10, 2011}}</ref> In February 2010, Sapolsky was named to the [[Freedom From Religion Foundation]]'s Honorary Board of distinguished achievers,<ref name="FFRFaward">{{cite web|title=Honorary FFRF Board Announced |url=http://ffrf.org/news/releases/honorary-ffrf-board-announced/|work=ffrf.org|access-date=February 15, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101217052917/http://ffrf.org/news/releases/honorary-ffrf-board-announced/|archive-date= December 17, 2010}}</ref> following the [[Emperor Has No Clothes Award]] for 2002.<ref>{{cite web|title=Emperor Has No Clothes Award -- Robert Sapolsky |date=September 2, 2002 |url=http://ffrf.org/outreach/awards/emperor-has-no-clothes-award/item/11897-robert-sapolsky |publisher=Freedom From Religion Foundation|access-date=7 December 2013}}</ref> In 2026, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref> {{Cite web
| url = https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/robert-sapolsky-sa14xg/
| title = Robert Sapolsky – NAS
| access-date = 6 November 2026
}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Sapolsky is married to Lisa Sapolsky, a doctor in [[neuropsychology]]. They have two children.<ref name="foot"/> In 2024, he launched a series of Father-Offspring Interviews on [[YouTube]] and [[Spotify]] with his daughter Rachel.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLOXn0rUD2D-eBMO44WUaxRFYqwv61pDaa|title= Father Offspring Interviews|last= Sapolsky|first= Robert|date= |via= YouTube|access-date= September 8, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Sapolsky |first=Robert |title=Father-Offspring Interviews |url=https://open.spotify.com/show/0wDrkkznSB8S84kKuK9HCo |access-date=2025-12-12 |website=Spotify |language=en}}</ref>

In his book ''[[Determined: A Science of Life Without Free Will]]'', Sapolsky discussed his personal experiences with [[Depression (mood)|depression]], revealing the complexities of living with the condition while also highlighting moments of relief provided by medication.<ref>{{cite book | title = [[Determined: A Science of Life Without Free Will]] | year = 2023 | first = Robert | last = Sapolsky | publisher = [[Penguin Press]] | page = 389}}</ref>

== Views ==
In a podcast interview with Light Watkins called "How To Escape The Rat Race",<ref>{{cite web |title=Neuroscientist: How To Escape The Rat Race with Robert Sapolsky | date=July 31, 2024 |via = [[YouTube]]|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PNMLlX7tyQk}}</ref> Sapolsky says that after learning in [[synagogue]] about how God "hardened Pharaoh's heart," he woke up one night at 2:00 a.m. as a teenager and said, "Oh, I get it! There is no god and there's no free will. The universe is this big, empty, indifferent place. And that's kinda where I've been at ever since."

==Further reading==
* * "Turtles All the Way Up" (review of [[Robert M. Sapolsky]], ''Determined: A Science of Life Without Free Will'', Penguin Press, 2023, 511 pp.), ''[[The New York Review of Books]]'', vol. LXXII, no. 2 (13 February 2025), pp. 23–25. The reviewer, [[Jessica Riskin]], writes: "[[Science]] can't prove there's no [[free will]] [Sapolsky's thesis is that there is no free will] because the question of free will is not a scientific question but a philosophical one. To misrepresent it as a scientific question is a prime example of [[scientism]] – of extending the claims of science beyond its bounds." (p. 25.)
